criticalActions.label: ECG correctly identified as anterior STEMI
IV access established and bloods drawn
Cath lab activated — primary PCI initiated

modifiers.description: Patient suffered a preventable cardiac arrest due to delayed management
Cardiogenic shock developed due to delayed reperfusion

start.hint: Crushing central chest pain with diaphoresis and jaw radiation in a middle-aged male with risk factors is an ACS until proven otherwise. The single fastest way to confirm what the heart is doing electrically takes about three minutes and should happen before anything else.
start.text:
EMS radio crackles: 'Inbound — 54-year-old male, construction foreman. Found by coworkers sitting on the ground. Severe central chest pain, diaphoretic, nauseous. Pain started 40 minutes ago while carrying materials. Pale and looks sick. BP 142/88, HR 98, SpO2 95%. ETA 3 minutes.'

Mr. Malcolm Torres rolls in on the stretcher, jaw clenched, hand pressed to his sternum. 'Doc, something is really wrong. I feel like there's a truck on my chest.'

Vitals confirmed: HR 98 | BP 142/88 | RR 20 | SpO2 95% | Temp 37.0°C | Pain 9/10

What is your first action?

choices.text: Order an immediate 12-lead ECG while attaching the monitor

effects.reason: 12-lead ECG ordered immediately — the single most important first step in undifferentiated chest pain

choices.text: Take a targeted chest pain history before any tests
Perform a rapid primary survey and physical examination
Establish IV access and draw bloods while attaching monitoring

effects.reason: IV access established and bloods drawn — appropriate supportive action
Bloods drawn before ECG delays the most critical diagnostic test in acute chest pain

history-hub.hint: History is valuable, but this presentation is already very suspicious for cardiac ischaemia. There is a standard electrical test that guidelines mandate within 10 minutes of any chest pain presentation — before labs, before detailed history.
history-hub.text:
Mr. Torres is in obvious discomfort but cooperative. You need to be efficient.

What history do you want?

choices.text: Character and onset of the chest pain
Cardiac risk factors and past medical history
Current medications and allergies
Screen for thrombolytic and antiplatelet contraindications
Review the ECG (already ordered)

effects.reason: ECG ordered after focused history — appropriate prioritisation

history-hpi.text:
9/10 crushing, pressure-like pain. Radiates to jaw and left arm. Onset 40 minutes ago, abrupt, while lifting heavy materials. Constant since. Nausea and profuse diaphoresis. Similar milder episode 2 days ago resolved at rest — he thought it was indigestion.

No pleuritic component. No positional change. No cough or dyspnoea preceding the pain.

choices.text: Continue taking history

history-risk-factors.text:
PMHx: Hypertension (8 years), Type 2 Diabetes (5 years). No prior MI, PCI, CABG, or known CAD.

Risk factors: Active smoker (30 pack-years). Father had fatal MI at 58. BMI 31. Elevated cholesterol known but untreated until 3 weeks ago.

Extremely high-risk cardiac profile.

choices.text: Continue taking history

history-medications.text:
Medications: Metformin 1g BD, Lisinopril 5mg OD, Atorvastatin 40mg OD (started 3 weeks ago).

Allergies: Penicillin (childhood rash — likely non-anaphylactic). No NSAID allergy. No warfarin, DOAC, or antiplatelet agents. No GTN prescription.

choices.text: Continue taking history

history-contraindications.text:
Contraindication screen:
- No recent surgery (dental extraction 2 years ago)
- No prior stroke, TIA, or intracranial pathology
- No active bleeding or coagulopathy
- BP 142/88 — below the thrombolytic threshold of 185/110

No contraindications to aspirin, anticoagulation, or thrombolysis if indicated.

choices.text: Continue taking history

rapid-exam.text:
Primary survey (90 seconds):

A: Patent, self-maintaining.
B: RR 20. Bilateral air entry. Fine bibasal crackles — early pulmonary oedema.
C: HR 98, regular. BP 142/88. Pallor, diaphoresis. Peripheral pulses present. Cap refill 2-3s.
D: GCS 15. Oriented. Pain 9/10.

Cardiovascular: S1 + S2 present. S4 gallop at apex (reduced LV compliance). No murmurs. JVP not elevated. Mild peripheral oedema (likely chronic).

The S4 gallop and bibasal crackles are highly significant in the context of acute chest pain.

choices.text: Review the ECG (already ordered)

effects.reason: ECG ordered after focused exam — appropriate next step

choices.text: Take focused history first

iv-access-node.text: Large-bore IV established. Bloods drawn (troponin, FBC, U&E, glucose, coag). The most important diagnostic question is on the ECG.

choices.text: Review the ECG (already ordered)

effects.reason: ECG ordered — required diagnostic first step

ecg-ordered.hint: 4mm ST elevation across the anterior leads (V1–V4) with reciprocal inferior depression is the textbook pattern for an anterior STEMI. Troponin is not needed to act — this ECG alone is enough to activate the cath lab. The heart muscle is dying right now.
ecg-ordered.text:
The 12-lead ECG is printed. Good quality, no artefact.

Systematic review:
Rate: 98 bpm | Rhythm: Regular sinus | Axis: Normal | PR: 160ms | QRS: 80ms (narrow)

ST segments:
[!] 4mm ST elevation in V1, V2, V3, V4 — anterior distribution
[!] Reciprocal ST depression in leads II, III, aVF
[!] Hyperacute broad-based T-waves in V2, V3

No Q-waves. No bundle branch block. No prior ECG for comparison.

How do you interpret this ECG?

choices.text: Anterior STEMI — 4mm STE in V1-V4 with reciprocal inferior changes. Activate STEMI pathway.

effects.reason: ECG correctly interpreted as anterior STEMI — confident, accurate identification

choices.text: Possible NSTEMI or unstable angina — order troponin and admit for observation

effects.reason: ECG misidentified as NSTEMI — 4mm STE in V1-V4 with reciprocal changes is diagnostic STEMI. Troponin is not required to activate the STEMI pathway.

choices.text: ST changes could be early repolarisation — repeat ECG in 30 minutes

effects.reason: CRITICAL ERROR — 4mm STE in V1-V4 with reciprocal ST depression cannot be early repolarisation. Early repolarisation is a diagnosis of exclusion in young patients with benign-appearing minimal changes. This is a life-threatening misdiagnosis.

choices.text: Widespread ST changes suggest pericarditis — order ESR, CRP, echocardiogram

effects.reason: Pericarditis causes diffuse saddle-shaped STE across many leads. Focal 4mm STE in V1-V4 with inferior reciprocal changes is the hallmark of transmural ischaemia, not inflammation.

misinterpretation-nstemi.text:
While waiting for the troponin, the ED nurse shows you the ECG again. 'Doctor — I've seen STEMIs before. The ST elevation is 4 millimetres in V2 with reciprocal inferior changes. Are you sure this isn't a STEMI?'

She's correct.

choices.text: She's right — re-interpret as anterior STEMI and activate the pathway immediately

effects.reason: STEMI correctly identified after reassessment — delayed but recovered

choices.text: Wait for the troponin — clinical decisions should not be based on nursing input

effects.reason: Dismissing valid nursing concern and waiting for troponin when ECG is diagnostic — a dangerous attitude that causes avoidable harm

misinterpretation-pericarditis.text:
You are completing the echo request when the cardiology registrar walks past and stops cold. 'Wait — that's not pericarditis. V1 to V4 with inferior reciprocal changes. That's an anterior STEMI. What is your door time?'

You have already lost 5 minutes. Mr. Torres' pain is 10/10.

choices.text: The cardiologist is correct — activate the STEMI pathway immediately

effects.reason: STEMI identified after specialist correction

stemi-confirmed.text:
ANTERIOR STEMI CONFIRMED.

Every passing minute costs ~1.7 years of life expectancy and ~1 billion cardiomyocytes.

Your team is assembled. The following can be delegated simultaneously:
• SpO2 95% — supplemental oxygen?
• Aspirin given?
• IV access and bloods done?
• Pain relief needed?
• Reperfusion strategy?

Your next action:

choices.text: Give supplemental oxygen — SpO2 95%

effects.reason: Oxygen given for SpO2 < 94% — guideline target 94-98%

choices.text: Administer aspirin 300mg chewable — no known allergy

effects.reason: Aspirin 300mg given — cornerstone antiplatelet therapy, reduces STEMI mortality ~25%

choices.text: Establish large-bore IV access and draw STEMI bloods

effects.reason: IV access established and STEMI bloods drawn — required for PCI preparation

choices.text: Give morphine 2.5mg IV for pain management

effects.reason: Analgesia given — reduces sympathetic activation. Use cautiously if haemodynamically unstable.

choices.text: Proceed to reperfusion decision — enough preparation

stemi-oxygen-given.text:
Oxygen via nasal cannula. SpO2 climbing toward 97%.

What next?

choices.text: Give aspirin 300mg chewable

effects.reason: Aspirin 300mg given

effects.reason: IV access established and bloods drawn

choices.text: Proceed to reperfusion decision

stemi-aspirin-given.text:
Mr. Torres chews the aspirin. 'That tasted awful.' Good — he can protect his airway.

What next?

effects.reason: Analgesia given

Large-bore IV in situ. Bloods sent. Troponin result in ~60 minutes.

What next?

stemi-analgesia-given.text:
Morphine 2.5mg IV given slowly. Pain falls from 9/10 to 7/10. He exhales shakily. 'Thank you.' Vitals stable.

What next?

choices.text: Give aspirin 300mg chewable

effects.reason: Aspirin 300mg given

choices.text: Give supplemental oxygen

effects.reason: Oxygen given for SpO2 < 94%

choices.text: Proceed to reperfusion decision

treatment-decision.text:
ANTERIOR STEMI. 24/7 interventional cardiology available on-site. No transfer required.

ACC/AHA / ESC Guidelines: Primary PCI preferred when achievable within 120 minutes of first medical contact. Door-to-balloon target: 90 min (ideally 60). Thrombolytics are second-line when PCI unavailable within 120 minutes.

Reperfusion strategy?

choices.text: Activate primary PCI — call the Cath Lab now

effects.reason: Primary PCI activated — gold standard with on-site catheterisation. Maximises myocardial salvage.

choices.text: Administer IV thrombolytics (alteplase/tPA) — start immediately

effects.reason: Thrombolytics chosen when primary PCI is available on-site — guideline-discordant. PCI produces superior outcomes when door-to-balloon is feasible within 120 minutes.

choices.text: Medical management only — he is haemodynamically stable for now

effects.reason: CRITICAL ERROR — medical management alone in acute STEMI carries 20-35% in-hospital mortality. Reperfusion therapy is mandatory unless absolutely contraindicated.

choices.text: Wait for the troponin result before committing to reperfusion

effects.reason: Waiting for troponin when ECG is diagnostic for STEMI is a critical error. The ECG alone dictates treatment — troponin confirms injury but does not gate reperfusion.

cath-lab-activated.text:
Cath Lab coordinator answers on the first ring. Interventional cardiologist already in the building — team assembles in 15 minutes. Door-to-balloon tracking: 35-45 minutes.

Nurse asks: 'Before we transfer — anticoagulation? P2Y12?'

choices.text: Full regimen: heparin 5000 units IV bolus + ticagrelor 180mg loading dose

effects.reason: Unfractionated heparin given pre-PCI — reduces thrombus propagation and periprocedural complications
Ticagrelor 180mg loading dose given — dual antiplatelet therapy is guideline class I for primary PCI

choices.text: Heparin 5000 units IV only — Cath Lab to decide on P2Y12

effects.reason: Heparin given — correct. P2Y12 loading ideally should be given pre-PCI.

choices.text: Transfer immediately — anticoagulation can be given in the Cath Lab

effects.reason: Pre-PCI anticoagulation reduces thrombus burden and improves procedural outcomes — should be given in the ED when feasible

choices.text: First — confirm aspirin has been given

aspirin-check.text:
The nurse confirms aspirin has not been given yet. 'Should I give it now?'

Aspirin reduces STEMI mortality by ~25%. No documented allergy.

choices.text: Yes — give aspirin 300mg immediately before transfer

effects.reason: Aspirin given before PCI — delayed but correct

choices.text: No — transfer now, Cath Lab can give it

effects.reason: Aspirin not given — mandatory critical action in STEMI. Mortality benefit too significant to omit.

pre-pci-complete.text:
Complete pre-PCI preparation: oxygen on, aspirin given, heparin infusing, ticagrelor loaded. IV running. Mr. Torres is ready. Porters at the door.

Door-to-balloon tracking: 38 minutes.

choices.text: Transfer to Cath Lab — go

pre-pci-partial.text: Heparin running. Mr. Torres ready for transfer. Door-to-balloon tracking: 42 minutes.

choices.text: Transfer to Cath Lab

pre-pci-no-anticoag.text: Mr. Torres being transferred without pre-PCI anticoagulation. Door-to-balloon within the 90-minute window.

choices.text: Transfer to Cath Lab

thrombolytics-pathway.text:
Alteplase running. At 20 minutes post-infusion: repeat ECG shows persistent 4mm ST elevation in V1-V4. No reduction. No reperfusion arrhythmia. No pain relief.

Failed thrombolysis.

The interventional cardiologist calls: 'We're scrubbed. Are you sending him up?'

choices.text: Transfer for rescue PCI — thrombolysis has failed

effects.reason: Rescue PCI appropriately initiated after failed thrombolysis — guideline-concordant
Cath Lab activated via rescue PCI pathway — delayed but correct

choices.text: Give a second dose of tPA — reinforce the first dose

effects.reason: CRITICAL ERROR — repeat thrombolysis after failed first dose is absolutely contraindicated. Dramatically increases bleeding risk with no benefit. Rescue PCI is the only correct response.

choices.text: Continue observation — give the drug more time

effects.reason: Failed thrombolysis not recognised — persistent STE at 20 minutes with no reperfusion signs mandates immediate rescue PCI

conservative-disaster.text:
One hour passes. Mr. Torres is deteriorating: HR 118, BP 102/64, SpO2 91%. Dyspnoeic. Increasingly confused.

'Doctor,' the nurse says quietly, 'he looks like he's in shock.'

Cardiogenic shock is developing.

choices.text: Activate Cath Lab — emergent PCI for STEMI with cardiogenic shock

effects.reason: Cath Lab activated — correct, though significantly delayed with shock already established

choices.text: Start IV fluids and vasopressors — stabilise before deciding

effects.reason: Vasopressors are a bridge to PCI — not a substitute. Emergent revascularisation is the definitive treatment. Further delay is fatal.

troponin-wait-disaster.text:
Sixty minutes pass. Troponin I: 48,220 ng/L (reference < 52 ng/L). Massively elevated.

Mr. Torres is drowsy. HR 126, BP 88/54, SpO2 88% on high-flow oxygen. Runs of non-sustained VT on the monitor.

Cardiogenic shock. This is now critical.

choices.text: Activate Cath Lab emergently — STEMI with cardiogenic shock

effects.reason: Cath Lab activated — 60 minutes too late. Shock established. Significant myocardium already lost.

cardiogenic-shock-delay.text: Mr. Torres deteriorates rapidly. BP 82/50. Barely conscious. The nurse is at the crash trolley. Cardiogenic shock fully established.

choices.text: Activate Cath Lab — emergent PCI for STEMI with cardiogenic shock

effects.reason: Cath Lab activated after significant delay — shock already established

catastrophic-delay.text: [ALERT] 30 minutes have elapsed waiting for a 'repeat ECG'. Mr. Torres is slumped in the trolley. Barely conscious. SpO2 89%. Senior nursing staff have called for help.

choices.text: Activate Cath Lab — this is a STEMI, the initial ECG interpretation was wrong

effects.reason: Cath Lab finally activated after a critical 30-minute delay — most viable myocardium already lost

vf-arrest-event.text: [CODE BLUE] Mr. Torres loses consciousness. The cardiac monitor alarms: coarse ventricular fibrillation. He is pulseless and unresponsive. The crash cart is 2 metres away.

choices.text: Call Code Blue — CPR immediately, charge defibrillator to 200J biphasic
Defibrillate immediately without starting CPR

effects.reason: CPR should be commenced while charging the defibrillator — minimise hands-off time

cardiogenic-shock-event.text: [DETERIORATION] Mr. Torres is in cardiogenic shock. BP 84/52. HR 122. Confused, diaphoretic. SpO2 dropping. Cardiomyocytes are dying en masse.

choices.text: Activate Cath Lab — emergent PCI mandatory in STEMI with cardiogenic shock

effects.reason: Cath Lab activated — significantly delayed but only chance for survival

choices.text: Start norepinephrine infusion to stabilise BP before Cath Lab

effects.reason: CRITICAL ERROR — vasopressors delay the only treatment that can save this patient. Vasopressors are a bridge to PCI, not a substitute.

deterioration-event.text: [DETERIORATION] Mr. Torres is increasingly distressed. HR 116, SpO2 dropping to 91%. He grabs the rail. 'Something's happening — doctor, please.' ECG shows worsening ischaemic changes extending to lateral leads.

choices.text: Activate Cath Lab — this STEMI requires urgent reperfusion
Attempt medical stabilisation before committing to an invasive strategy

effects.reason: Continued delay in the face of clinical deterioration — reperfusion cannot be further deferred

resuscitation.text: CPR in progress. Defibrillator shows coarse VF. Two minutes of CPR completed. Rhythm check: still VF. The team looks to you.

choices.text: 200J biphasic — CLEAR — shock delivered

effects.reason: Prompt defibrillation for VF — correct and timely

choices.text: Give amiodarone 300mg IV before shocking

effects.reason: Amiodarone before the first shock in VF is not recommended — defibrillation takes priority in cycles 1 and 2. Amiodarone is indicated after the third failed shock.

rosc-achieved.text:
ROSC — return of spontaneous circulation after 1 shock. Sinus rhythm. HR 86, BP 92/58. Mr. Torres responds to commands — confused but alive.

Interventional cardiologist on the phone: 'We're scrubbed. Bring him up — we'll open the artery now.'

choices.text: Transfer to Cath Lab — post-arrest STEMI mandates emergent PCI

effects.reason: Primary PCI after ROSC in STEMI — guideline class I recommendation. Correct, though a preventable arrest precedes it.

choices.text: Stabilise in ICU first — catheterise when he is more stable

effects.reason: Post-arrest STEMI patients should proceed directly to the Cath Lab if haemodynamically stable — the ischaemic window is closing.

outcome-excellent.text:
Mr. Torres is wheeled into Cath Lab 1 with quiet efficiency. The interventional cardiologist threads a catheter through the radial artery. The coronary angiogram reveals a 95% occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery — the widow-maker.

A drug-eluting stent is deployed. TIMI-3 flow restored. ST segments resolve within minutes. Pain: 0/10.

--- Results ---
Door-to-balloon time: 38 minutes
Peak troponin I: 6,400 ng/L (small infarct for the LAD territory)
Echo Day 2: EF 58%. No significant wall motion abnormality. Anterior wall preserved.
Discharge: Day 3.

Mr. Torres shakes your hand at the door. 'My daughter's wedding is in June. I'll be there because of you.'

outcome-good.text:
Primary PCI performed successfully. Door-to-balloon: 46 minutes — within guidelines.

LAD stented. TIMI-3 flow. ST segments resolve.

--- Results ---
Peak troponin I: 12,800 ng/L
Echo Day 2: EF 52%, mild anterior hypokinesis
Discharge: Day 4

Full recovery expected with cardiac rehabilitation. Pre-procedural P2Y12 loading would have reduced thrombus burden — a measurable missed opportunity.

outcome-suboptimal.text:
Primary PCI completed. Door-to-balloon: 55 minutes.

Good outcome — not optimal. Absence of pre-procedural anticoagulation led to higher thrombus burden requiring aspiration thrombectomy before stenting.

--- Results ---
Peak troponin I: 18,400 ng/L
Echo Day 2: EF 49%, anterior hypokinesis
Discharge: Day 5

His ejection fraction reflects the consequence of every omitted step.

outcome-rescue-pci.text:
Rescue PCI successful. Proximal LAD stented — TIMI-3 flow achieved after aspiration thrombectomy.

Thrombolytics partially disrupted the clot but failed reperfusion (~30% of cases). Delay in recognising lytic failure extended the ischaemic window significantly.

--- Results ---
Peak troponin I: 52,000 ng/L
Echo Day 2: EF 44%, moderate anterior wall motion abnormality
Discharge: Day 7 on heart failure therapy

He survives, but his heart will work harder for the rest of his life.

outcome-shock-pci.text:
Emergency PCI performed in cardiogenic shock. LAD opened, but downstream myocardium has suffered prolonged ischaemia.

--- Results ---
Post-procedure EF: 32%
ICU: 4 days — inotropic support and mechanical ventilation
Discharge: Day 14 — severe systolic dysfunction

Lifelong heart failure therapy required. ICD implantation. Significant functional limitations.

Reperfusion delay is the cause. Time is muscle. Muscle is life.

outcome-complicated.text:
PCI performed post-resuscitation. LAD stented. TIMI-3 flow — but the ischaemic window was extended by a preventable cardiac arrest.

--- Results ---
Post-procedure EF: 36%
ICU: 8 days — intubated, vasoactive support
Discharge: Severe cardiomyopathy requiring ICD and GDMT

He survives. But the arrest caused hypoxic injury beyond the myocardium. A preventable deterioration produced a survivable but life-altering complication.

outcome-fatal.text:
Mr. Malcolm Torres does not survive.

Refractory cardiogenic shock — despite late resuscitation attempts — results in multi-organ failure. The myocardium, deprived of reperfusion for too long, cannot recover.

Time of death is called.

─────────────────

Every minute of delay in STEMI costs approximately 1.7 years of life expectancy. The 90-minute door-to-balloon target exists because of cases like this one.

The decisions that led here were reversible. Review this case and identify the branch point where the outcome changed.
